name: Distributed System

units.title: Introduction, Goals, Architectures and Naming
topics: Seeing distributed systems: hardware, architecture and numbers

sections.title: Seeing distributed systems: hardware, architecture and numbers

summary: A distributed system is autonomous nodes cooperating by messages to look like one system; it has concurrency, no global clock and independent failures.
Goals: resource sharing, transparency (access, location, migration, replication, concurrency, failure), openness, scalability (size, geography, administration) and dependability.
Serial availability multiplies (five 99.9% services give 99.5010%); parallel replicas raise it as 1 − (1 − a)ⁿ; latency is bounded by distance.
Architectures: client-server (tiers), P2P (unstructured, structured DHT, hybrid); middleware hides heterogeneity.
Chord places keys on a ring with O(log N) lookup; DNS combines partitioning and replication.
Models: synchronous, asynchronous, partially synchronous; failures: crash, omission, timing, Byzantine. FLP forbids guaranteed deterministic consensus under asynchrony.

units.title: Communication: Sockets, RPC, RMI, gRPC and Message Queues
topics: Seeing communication: wires, handshakes, stubs and queues

sections.title: Seeing communication: wires, handshakes, stubs and queues

summary: Sockets expose TCP streams (reliable, ordered, need framing) and UDP datagrams (lossy, message-preserving); TCP's reliability does not replace end-to-end application acknowledgements.
Marshalling fixes byte order and layout: the 11-byte fixed record and the 35-byte JSON for the same data; protobuf varints encode 150 as 96 01 and 300 as ac 02.
RPC hides communication behind stubs, but the caller must still handle timeouts; at-least-once plus a request ID gives at-most-once. The retry experiment charged 300 instead of 100 without dedup.
RMI passes remote references; gRPC uses protobuf over HTTP/2 with unary and streaming calls and deadlines.
Message queues decouple sender and receiver in time and space; at-least-once delivery means duplicates and reordering, so handlers must be idempotent.

units.title: Time, Clocks and Global State
topics: Seeing time: clocks, clock servers and event diagrams

sections.title: Seeing time: clocks, clock servers and event diagrams

summary: Physical clocks drift at ρ (about 10 ppm = 0.864 s/day); synchronisation must repeat about every δ/2ρ.

Cristian: estimate = Tₛ + RTT/2, accuracy ± (RTT/2 − min). Berkeley: average clock differences and send each node its adjustment. NTP: θ = ((t₁−t₀)+(t₂−t₃))/2, δ = (t₃−t₀) − (t₂−t₁); path asymmetry remains as error.
Happened-before is a partial order; Lamport clocks give L(a) < L(b) whenever a → b but not the converse; vector clocks give a → b ⇔ V(a) < V(b) and expose concurrency.

units.title: Coordination: Mutual Exclusion and Leader Election
topics: In practice: leases and coordination services
Seeing coordination: shared hardware, quorums and elections

sections.title: In practice: leases and coordination services
Seeing coordination: shared hardware, quorums and elections

summary: Mutual exclusion must be safe, live and fair; compare algorithms by messages and delay.

Centralised: 3 messages; Ricart–Agrawala: 2(N − 1) messages and a timestamp order (24 messages for N = 4 in the simulation); Maekawa: about 3√N messages using intersecting quorums; token ring: token hops, with loss to handle.
Bully: highest live id wins; best case 6 messages, worst case 41 for N = 7 with the top process dead. Ring: 2 × live processes = 12 messages.
Leases and fencing tokens plus consensus-backed services replace hand-written algorithms in practice.

units.title: Distributed Transactions and Concurrency Control
topics: Seeing transactions: logs, graphs and compensations

sections.title: Seeing transactions: logs, graphs and compensations

summary: Distributed atomic commit uses a coordinator; 2PC votes then decides and costs 4N messages for N participants (12 for N = 3), but blocks when the coordinator crashes in the READY state.
3PC adds PRE-COMMIT and avoids blocking only under synchrony; modern systems use consensus-replicated commit instead.
A schedule is conflict-serializable iff its precedence graph is acyclic; strict 2PL guarantees it; timestamp ordering and optimistic control are alternatives.
Distributed deadlocks are cycles in the global wait-for graph; edge chasing detects them with probes; wait-die and wound-wait prevent them.
Sagas replace distributed ACID with local transactions plus compensation.

units.title: Replication, Consistency Models and Consensus
topics: Seeing replication: copies, quorums, proposals and logs

sections.title: Seeing replication: copies, quorums, proposals and logs

summary: Replicate for availability, performance and fault tolerance; state machine replication keeps replicas identical by ordering commands through consensus.
Models: linearizable ⊃ sequential ⊃ causal ⊃ eventual (in strength). A stale read after a completed write is sequentially consistent but not linearizable (H2).
CAP: under partition choose consistency or availability; PACELC adds latency vs consistency otherwise.
Quorums: R + W > N forces intersection; enumeration found 10 disjoint pairs for (N, W, R) = (5, 2, 3) and none for (5, 3, 3).
Paxos is safe because a new proposer must adopt the highest accepted value from its majority; Raft uses terms, randomised timeouts, majority commit and the current-term rule.

units.title: Fault Tolerance and Distributed File Systems
topics: Seeing failure: walls, disks, racks and snapshots

sections.title: Seeing failure: walls, disks, racks and snapshots

summary: Redundancy is the basis of fault tolerance; failure detectors suspect silent nodes by timeout; crash tolerance needs 2f + 1 replicas for majorities, Byzantine tolerance 3f + 1.
OM(1) works for n = 4 and fails validity for n = 3 with one traitor; PBFT quorums are 2f + 1 of 3f + 1.
Chandy–Lamport records a consistent global state (90 + 55 + 5 = 150 here); checkpointing avoids the domino effect when coordinated.
NFS is stateless with close-to-open consistency; AFS caches whole files with callbacks; GFS/HDFS use a master plus large replicated blocks with rack-aware placement.
